title: Your writing was flagged as AI. What does that actually mean?

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A university writing center tutor and a graduate student discuss a submission flagged by an AI detector.

script.en: Hi, Professor Lin. Thanks for seeing me on such short notice. I'm really worried about my dissertation chapter.
Of course, Mei. Come in. What's happened? You look quite distressed.

Well, I submitted a draft to the journal you recommended, and yesterday I got an email saying their screening tool had flagged it as possibly AI-generated. I've never used AI for my writing. Not once.
I see. That must have been alarming. Did they reject it outright?

Not exactly. The editor said the detector result wasn't the sole reason, but she asked me to explain how I'd written it, and she hinted that I might need to provide drafts or notes. I don't know what to send. I write directly on my laptop.

That's a common problem. These detectors analyze patterns—sentence rhythm, word choice, punctuation. They're not actually reading your mind. And they do produce false positives, especially for non-native speakers whose prose is very regular.
So it's not just me? I was starting to think I must have done something wrong without realizing it.

No, you're not alone. I read a study recently where researchers tested four detectors on academic papers. Even the best one missed some cases and misidentified others. The tools are useful for triage, but they shouldn't be treated as judges.
But what can I do now? The editor wants evidence. I can't prove a negative.

You can provide your earlier outlines, maybe your reading notes, and offer to discuss the argument in person. Also, ask the editor which tool was used and whether a human reviewed the result. Sometimes a conversation resolves it.
That's helpful. I do have outlines and some handwritten notes. I'll gather them today.
Good. And don't let this make you second-guess your own voice. The burden shouldn't be on you to prove you're human, but until policies change, we have to work with what we have.

script.en: In recent years, as artificial intelligence writing tools have become widely accessible, publishers and editors have faced a rising tide of submissions. To cope, many have adopted automated detection software designed to distinguish human prose from machine output. These tools promise efficiency, but their limitations are becoming increasingly apparent. Detection systems typically analyze textual features such as sentence length, vocabulary diversity, and punctuation habits. They compare these patterns against models of how humans and machines are thought to write, and the problem is that human writing is enormously varied. A scholar who favors formal syntax, a journalist who uses em dashes, or a student whose first language is not English may all produce text that resembles machine output according to a detector's criteria. False positives—cases where human work is wrongly flagged—can have serious consequences. Writers may lose opportunities, face damaged reputations, or be forced to defend their integrity without knowing what triggered the alarm. Because detection algorithms are proprietary, accused authors often cannot examine the evidence against them. This asymmetry places a heavy burden on the accused, and some institutions have responded by requiring multiple layers of review. Rather than relying on a single score, editors may ask for drafts, notes, or an interview with the author. Others have chosen to abandon detection altogether, arguing that the technology is not yet reliable enough for high-stakes decisions. Meanwhile, researchers continue to improve the tools, though even developers acknowledge that no system is foolproof. The broader lesson may be that technology alone cannot resolve questions of authorship. Detection tools can help human judgment, but they cannot replace it. As long as institutions treat algorithmic scores as definitive proof, the risk of injustice will remain. A balanced approach—using detectors as one signal among many—seems more defensible than either blind trust or outright rejection.

sections.title: When AI Detectors Get It Wrong
sections.passage: Ghostwriter Sally McGraw hoped to land a job developing a book proposal for a client. After submitting a writing sample, she received an unexpected reply: an email stating that multiple AI detection tools had flagged her work as machine-generated. "I was floored because I had not used AI," McGraw said. "I'd written it all myself." The client later confirmed she had screened the sample for AI but said the results were not the determining factor in hiring another writer, citing experience and fit instead. McGraw believes the detector results cost her the opportunity. As editors struggle with a growing influx of AI-generated content, some turn to detection tools to sift through mounting submissions. But these tools are imperfect: they have falsely flagged human-written work as AI, leaving writers with little idea of what triggered the result or how to prove otherwise. In 2021, one publication received roughly 1,100 submissions a month. By February 2023, after AI agents such as ChatGPT became widely available, that number had doubled, forcing the outlet to temporarily close its submission portal. While AI detectors have grown more sophisticated, the companies behind them acknowledge the tools are not foolproof. Researchers have found that different detectors can reach dramatically different conclusions about the same piece of writing. In a June study in the International Journal for Educational Integrity, researchers compared four widely used detectors on 160 academic papers, including human-written texts and AI material rewritten by humans. Among the four, Pangram was most consistently accurate, correctly identifying AI use in 37 of 40 papers with combined text and in 37 of 40 papers where a human rewrote AI-generated text. "Many AI detectors work by asking a large language model how predictable a passage is," Callison-Burch said. "The catch is that the language models also tend to find text from their training data unusually predictable." That may explain what science blogger Janelle Shane encountered in late 2022 when she tested excerpts from her 2019 book about how AI works. One detector reported 98.7% confidence that a passage was machine-generated, and "This is a clear, glaring, blinking-light false positive," Shane said. "I had written this text myself." Detectors look for clues in word choice, punctuation and sentence structure. The word "delve," frequent em dashes, and ideas grouped in threes can trigger an AI-positive result. So can opening sentences with adverbs such as "notably" or "crucially," or posing a question immediately followed by answering it. Yet those are familiar habits for human writers. Callison-Burch notes that detectors weigh patterns across a whole piece, so an em dash or a particular word alone does not necessarily mean a bot was used. The Authors Guild, which advocates for writers' rights, said in May that the use of AI detectors "creates an environment reminiscent of witch hunts," with writers worried about false accusations and how to defend themselves. "A false positive can cost an author their publishing contract and reputation," the Guild wrote. Clarke, a sci-fi magazine publisher, occupies a middle ground.

long_sentences.en: "The catch is that the language models also tend to find text from their training data unusually predictable." That could explain what science blogger Janelle Shane encountered in late 2022 when she tested excerpts from her 2019 book about how AI works, You Look Like a Thing and I Love You .

"A false positive can cost an author their publishing contract and reputation, and a false negative, when AI-generated work slips through reputable publishing undetected, can cause readers to lose their trust in authors and the industry," the Guild wrote .

Among the four detectors, Pangram was the most consistently accurate, correctly identifying the use of AI in 37 of the 40 papers with the combined text and in 37 of the 40 papers where a human rewrote AI-generated text.
